title: How to change the default font in Google Docs on Mac: browser steps for new docs
metaTitle: How to Change the Default Font in Google Docs on Mac
description: Learn how to change the default font in Google Docs on Mac using the Format menu in your browser, then save it so new documents use it.
targetKeyword: how to change the default font in google docs on mac
secondaryKeywords: change default font google docs mac
intro: To change the default font in Google Docs on Mac, set the font on body text, update the Normal text style to match, then save it as your default. Open Format > Paragraph styles > Options and choose Save as my default styles, and new documents will use that font from then on.
tldr: Set the font on body text, not a heading, in the browser version of Google Docs.
Apply Normal text, then choose Format > Paragraph styles > Normal text > Update 'Normal text' to match.
Choose Format > Paragraph styles > Options > Save as my default styles so new documents use the font.
Google's help page does not say whether existing documents change, so test on a copy first.

blocks.text: What the default font actually controls

When you pick a font from the toolbar, you change the text you have selected. You do not change the default. Google Docs stores body text formatting in a paragraph style called Normal text. That style controls the text you type when nothing else is chosen. Update Normal text, save it, and the default changes.

Think of a style as a saved recipe. Every paragraph that uses Normal text follows the recipe. Change the recipe once, and the paragraphs that use it pick up the change. That is why you fix the style instead of formatting each paragraph by hand.

No native Google Docs app for macOS turned up in Google's documentation, so these steps assume you use Docs in a browser. Google's pages do not show Mac-specific menu differences, so the paths below should match what you see. If your menu names look different, compare them against the paths here before you change anything.
Before you start

items: A Google Doc open in your browser, not a preview or a downloaded file.
Edit access to the document. If someone else owns the file, ask them to make the change or make a copy first.
The font you want. Find it in the font box in the toolbar before you start.
A short sample: two lines of body text and one heading, so you can see each change as it happens.

blocks.text: The sample is test text you control. Use a copy of the file if the original matters to you. You will select the sample several times, and the selection is what the menus act on.
Step by step: set the Normal text style

Work through the steps in order. The first three update the style. The last two save it for new documents and check the result. The table below lists the same paths, so you can scan them before you start.

rows: Update Normal text to match your sample
Format > Paragraph styles > Normal text > Update 'Normal text' to match
Save the style for new documents
Format > Paragraph styles > Options > Save as my default styles
blocks.caption: Paths follow Google's help page and the 2019 How-To Geek guide. Shortcuts come from Google's keyboard list.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Say you want Georgia for body text. Select one sentence of body text, apply Normal text, choose Georgia in the font box, and keep the size you want. Then update the Normal text style. Every new paragraph you type after that starts in Georgia.

A quick note on the Format shortcut. Google lists Ctrl + Option + O to open the Format menu. Some search snippets list Command + Option + F, which does not match Google's page. Use Google's version when they disagree.
Why the Normal text style matters

Body text fills most documents. Notes, drafts, memos and essays all run on Normal text. When that style is right, nearly every paragraph you type starts in the font you chose. You skip the step of formatting each paragraph by hand.

Pasting is where the default can get messy. Text copied from a web page or another file may keep its own font. Check the font after you paste, and apply Normal text again if the pasted text does not match the rest of the body.
When to change the default and when to leave it

Change the default when you write most of your documents in one font. A personal template, a class paper, or a set of meeting notes all benefit. If a teacher, editor or client gives you a required font, use their font for their files and skip this change for those documents.

A simple test helps. Count how many new documents you start from blank in a typical month. If the answer is more than a handful, set the default once. If you rarely start from blank, a template may serve you better, and the template guide below explains how to build one.
Change heading fonts too

Headings are separate styles. Changing Normal text does not touch Heading 1, Heading 2 or Title. A 2019 guide from How-To Geek describes the same method for each heading style. Pick the heading, set its font, then open Format > Paragraph styles > [style] and choose Update '[style]' to match.

For a Title, the path reads Format > Paragraph styles > Title > Update 'Title' to match. Think about which headings you actually use. A memo may need only Heading 2, while a thesis may need all of them. Set the headings you use and skip the rest. Check the size and weight on each heading too, not just the font name. The guide is from 2019, so check the menu names on your screen before you rely on it.
Check that new documents use your font
Test the change before you rely on it. Open File > New > Document, type one sentence and one heading, and look at the font box. If the body text uses your font and size, the default is saved.

Look at two things. First, the font box should show your font when the cursor sits in a body paragraph. Second, the heading you typed should keep its own style and not turn into body text. If either check fails, go back to the options step rather than changing the sample again.

If the new document still uses the old font, go back to Format > Paragraph styles > Options. Choose Save as my default styles again. Google's help page says this applies to new documents, so a fresh blank file is the right test.
Existing documents: what changes and what does not

Google's help page says the saved default applies to new documents. It does not say whether existing documents change. Some third-party snippets tell you to select all text and use Use my default styles to update old files. Google's page does not mention that option, so treat it as unverified.

The safe move is to test on a copy. Make a copy of the old file, update the sample text in the copy, and check the result. If the copy looks right, you can decide whether the original needs the same change. For the copy steps, see [how to make a copy of a document in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/make-a-copy-of-a-document-in-google-docs).
Mistakes people make with the default font

items: Changing the toolbar font and stopping there. That only changes the text you selected.
Updating Normal text but skipping Save as my default styles. The open document changes, and new documents do not.
Using a heading as the sample. You then change a heading style and not Normal text.
Assuming old files will change. Google's help page does not confirm that.
Forgetting the headings. Title and Heading 1 keep their old fonts until you update them.
Trusting a shortcut from a search snippet. Use the key combinations from Google's keyboard page.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes share one cause. The change worked in one place, and nobody checked a fresh document. Check a new blank document and a copy of an old file, and you catch the problem early.
Keyboard shortcuts for faster formatting
Shortcuts speed up the whole job. Google's keyboard page lists these Mac shortcuts for text formatting. ⌘ + B makes text bold, ⌘ + I makes it italic, and ⌘ + U underlines it.

items: ⌘ + Option + 1 to 6: apply Heading 1 to Heading 6
Ctrl + Option + O: open the Format menu

blocks.text: Copy formatting and paste formatting pair well with the default. Copy the look of a heading you already styled and paste it onto a new heading. You avoid reopening menus for every line.
Google's page warns that some shortcuts might not work for all languages or keyboards. If a shortcut does nothing, use the menu path instead. The menu is the reliable fallback.
Edge cases: long files, shared files and languages

A Google Doc can hold up to 1.02 million characters, according to Google Drive Help. Most documents stay far below that. A long manuscript or a merged report may come closer, which is a reason to set styles early so the whole file stays consistent.
Shared files add a limit. If you only have view or comment access, you cannot change the style. Ask the owner to make the change, or make your own copy and set the default there.
Language and keyboard layout matter too. Google's shortcut page notes that shortcuts can vary, so a Mac with a non-US keyboard may need the menu path for some steps.
What to do next

Once the default is set, many people turn next to layout. Headers, footers and page numbers are common next steps. The guide to [adding a header and footer in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/add-a-header-and-footer-in-google-docs) covers those menus.

If you write the same kind of document often, save it as a template instead of setting the font again. The steps are in [how to create a template in Google Docs on Mac](/how-to/create-a-template-in-google-docs). Students can also read [Google Docs for students on Mac](/for/students/google-docs).

faq.question: Does changing the default font change my existing Google Docs?
faq.answer: Google's help page says the saved default applies to new documents. It does not say whether existing documents change, so test on a copy first. Some third-party snippets mention an Update option for old files, but Google's page does not confirm it.

faq.question: Do I have to change heading fonts separately?
faq.answer: Yes. Headings have their own styles, so changing Normal text does not change them. A 2019 How-To Geek guide describes updating each heading style with Update 'Style' to match. Confirm the menu names on your own screen.

faq.question: Is there a native Google Docs app for Mac?
faq.answer: No native Google Docs app for macOS turned up in Google's documentation, so these steps cover Google Docs in your browser. Google's pages do not show Mac-specific menu differences either.

faq.question: What is the Normal text style?
faq.answer: Normal text is the paragraph style for body text. It sets the font that new body text uses. You change it through Format > Paragraph styles > Normal text, then update it to match your sample.

faq.question: Why did my font change only one paragraph?
faq.answer: The toolbar font box changes the text you have selected. To change the default, update the Normal text style, then save it with Save as my default styles under Format > Paragraph styles > Options.

faq.question: Which shortcut applies Normal text on a Mac?
faq.answer: Google's keyboard page lists ⌘ + Option + 0 for Normal text. The same page lists Ctrl + Option + O to open the Format menu. Some search snippets show other combinations, so use Google's list.

faq.question: How long can a Google Doc be?
faq.answer: Google Drive Help says a Google Doc can hold up to 1.02 million characters. Most documents stay far below that. Set your styles early so a very long file stays consistent.

steps.name: Apply the Normal text style to your sample
steps.text: Click into a line of ordinary body text, not a heading. Select that line, then go to Format > Paragraph styles > Normal text. The shortcut ⌘ + Option + 0 does the same thing.
steps.tip: Press Ctrl + Option + O to open the Format menu from the keyboard, as listed on Google's shortcut page.

steps.name: Set the font and size on the sample
steps.text: With the sample still selected, open the font box in the toolbar and choose your font. Set the size too. For example, choose Georgia and keep the size you want for body text.
steps.tip: The update in the next step copies the font you set here, so check that it looks right first.

steps.name: Update Normal text to match your sample
steps.text: Keep the sample selected. Go to Format > Paragraph styles > Normal text, then choose Update 'Normal text' to match. Docs copies the font you set into the Normal text style.
steps.tip: This step changes the style in the open document. The next step saves it for new documents.

steps.name: Open the Paragraph styles options
steps.text: Go to Format > Paragraph styles > Options. This is the step that saves your choice for future documents. Skip it, and new files may keep the old font.

steps.name: Choose Save as my default styles
steps.text: Select Save as my default styles. Google's help page says this sets the default for new documents. Repeat this step any time you change the Normal text style and want new files to match.
steps.tip: Google's help page does not show a confirmation message, so check a new document instead of waiting for one.

steps.name: Check a new blank document
steps.text: Open a new blank document from File > New > Document. Type one sentence and one heading. Confirm the body text uses your font and size, and the heading keeps its own style.
steps.tip: A blank new document is the test that matters, because Google's help page ties the saved default to new documents.

steps.name: Check an older document on a copy
steps.text: Make a copy of an older document, then look at its body text. Google's help page does not say whether existing documents change, so the copy is the safest way to see what happens in your file.
steps.tip: Make the copy first so the original file stays exactly as it was.

troubleshooting.problem: New documents still use the old font
troubleshooting.fix: Go to Format > Paragraph styles > Options and choose Save as my default styles. Updating Normal text alone changes the open document, and Google's help page ties the default to new documents.

troubleshooting.problem: The heading font did not change
troubleshooting.fix: Headings are separate styles. Set the font on that heading, then choose Format > Paragraph styles > [style] > Update '[style]' to match for each heading you use.

troubleshooting.problem: An old document still shows the old font
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help page does not say whether existing documents change. Check a copy first. If the old font stays, select the text you need and apply the font by hand from the toolbar.
Google's keyboard page says some shortcuts might not work for all languages or keyboards. Click Format in the Google Docs menu bar, or use the menu path instead.

troubleshooting.problem: A search snippet says Command + Option + F opens Format
troubleshooting.fix: Google's keyboard page lists Ctrl + Option + O for the Format menu. Use that combination, or click Format in the menu bar.

troubleshooting.problem: The Reset Styles option is missing
troubleshooting.fix: A 2019 How-To Geek guide mentions Reset Styles in the Options menu. Google's help page does not list it, so check your own menu before you rely on it.
